title: Five forms (CCC 2626–2643)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary prays: her fiat, be it done to me, and her Magnificat. Your line was yes, then praise.

One kitchen, one ordinary day, two people who love each other. Good morning, glad you're here. Could you grab milk on the way home? Call your sister, she's having a hard week. Thank you for dinner. And once, out of nowhere: you're amazing, you know that? Greeting, asking, asking for someone else, thanks, and plain admiration. Nobody learns those as categories. They're just what love sounds like. The Catechism names the same shapes in prayer.
screen: `GOOD MORNING. COULD YOU GRAB MILK?` → `CALL YOUR SISTER.` → `THANK YOU. YOU'RE AMAZING.`

segments.voice: First, blessing and adoration. Blessing, the Catechism says, is a meeting of God and the person: God blesses, and the heart blesses back the source of every blessing. Adoration is the creature standing before the Creator, and knowing it. Second, petition: asking. Asking shows we know what we are: creatures, not our own beginning. And the first thing to ask for is forgiveness, then the kingdom, before anything else. Third, intercession: asking for someone else. This is what Jesus does for us, and Christian intercession has no boundaries; it reaches even enemies. Fourth, thanksgiving. Every event and every need can become an offering of thanks, and the Catechism quotes the line from Paul you met in year two, in the Douay-Rheims: "In all things give thanks." It ties thanksgiving to the Eucharist, whose Greek name means thanksgiving. Fifth, praise, and here the Catechism draws a fine line. Praise gives God glory for his own sake, beyond anything he does, simply because he is. Thanks answers a gift; praise, in that picture, asks for nothing. And the Eucharist gathers all of them into one. The week in one breath: they shall see God; enough; God thirsts that we thirst; the long school; he prayed first; yes, then praise; and now, five ways to speak.
screen: `BLESSING AND ADORATION.` · `PETITION, THEN INTERCESSION.` · `THANKSGIVING: IN ALL THINGS.` · `PRAISE: FOR WHO GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Take each form for a few breaths, in your own words: blessing, noticing you stand before something larger than you; petition, one thing you need; intercession, one person who needs something; thanksgiving, one thing from today. Then praise: if you pray, say something to God that asks for nothing at all. If you don't pray, walk through the five as ways of paying attention.
Five forms. Blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise: in Catholic teaching, the shapes prayer takes, all gathered into the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: five ways to speak. Love already knows most of them by heart. That's the week.

howItsDone: The Mass holds the forms of prayer together: praise in the Gloria, petition and intercession in the prayers of the faithful, and thanksgiving in the Eucharistic Prayer.

chat.says: Isn't prayer basically just asking God for stuff?
options: Asking is one form; the Catechism names five: blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanks and praise.
Yes. The Catechism treats every prayer as a request, even thanks, which is really asking for more.
No. Asking is discouraged; the Catechism says real prayer only ever praises God and asks nothing.
chat.meaning: The Catechism names blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving and praise, and says the Eucharist gathers them all.

notes: CCC paraphrased throughout (copyrighted translation). Check: blessing as encounter and adoration as the creature's first attitude (2626–2628); petition, asking forgiveness first, then the kingdom (2629–2632); intercession with no boundaries, even enemies (2634–2636); thanksgiving and the Eucharist, 1 Thess 5:18 (2637–2638); praise for God's own sake (2639); the Eucharist containing all forms (2643).

'Praise, in that picture, asks for nothing': CCC 2639 says praise is the form of prayer that recognizes most immediately that God is God and gives him glory for his own sake; the script says only that praise asks for nothing. Confirm.
'The Eucharist, whose Greek name means thanksgiving' follows CCC 1328 and 2637; confirm.
